question: Following the investigation launched in 2023, on 4 December 2025 the Commission imposed a EUR 120 million fine on X for failure to comply with various transparency requirements established in the Digital Services Act.

Specifically, the failures highlighted were: the deceptive design of X’s ‘blue checkmark’ (Article 25(1)), the lack of transparency of X’s ads repository (Article 39) and the failure to provide researchers with access to public data (Article 40(12)).

According to the Commission, the level of the fine was determined taking account of the nature of the infringements, their gravity in relation to the number of affected users in the EU, and their duration. Considering the above: 1.
Can the Commission set out the criteria used for determining the level of the fine in detail?

As regards the infringement of Article 25(1), the Commission considers that the check mark can lead to errors. However, X announced changes to their verification system, replacing it with a more reliable one, which is linked to registered accounts and with easily accessible information. Therefore, on what criteria did the Commission base its conclusion that X had ifailed to comply with said article?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.2.2026) The Commission set three separate fines for each of the infringements by the provider of X of the Digital Services Act (DSA)1, namely for Article 25(1), 39 and 40(12) DSA, amounting to a total of EUR 120 million now due for payment.

2 The calculation of the fine for each infringement was based on the nature, gravity, recurrence and duration of the infringements, as well as potential aggravating and mitigating factors. The Commission considered objective criteria, in particular the impact of the specific breaches on the effectiveness of the DSA and their consequences for users, researchers and the public across the EU.
Other important factors were the duration of the infringements, and the need to ensure a sufficient deterrence effect. The turnover of the provider is not the starting point for determining the fine.

Instead, the turnover of the provider is used as a means of ensuring that the fines imposed are below the maximum ceiling for fines under the DSA (6% of the total worldwide annual turnover of a provider in the preceding financial year).

The Commission’s assessment regarding Article 25(1) DSA is based on a careful analysis of the processes the provider of X put in place to assess the authenticity of applicants to the ‘blue checkmark’ feature - which the provider of X explained to the Commission in detail upon request. It also considered third-party evidence and domain expertise on the efficiency of these safeguards.

Based on this assessment, the Commission concluded that the ‘blue checkmarks’ feature deceived users because any recipient could pay to obtain the ‘verified account’ status without the provider of X meaningfully verifying who was behind the account.
1 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single

Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act), OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, p. 1–102. 2 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-fines-x-eu120-million-under-digital-services-act.
